title: Desiderata for the Theory of Agents
raw_summary: TLDR: I give informal conceptual desiderata for the theory of agents we need to solve ASI alignment, and show a few examples of how existing theories fall short of these desiderata. A Theory of What? The word "agent" is often used in the AI safety discourse and in other research communities, but the intended meaning and scope of this concept varies substantially. For the purpose of this sequence, I informally define an agent to be a system with inputs ("observations") and outputs ("actions") that is effective at steering its environment in the direction of particular preferences, for a large variety of different environments. To do so, it arguably has to create a sophisticated model of the environment [1] , and use this model to build a long-term plan. Moreover, it has to continually update the model and revise the plan with new information and additional processing time. Additionally, it has to accomplish all of that while making efficient use of the available information (statistical efficiency) and computing resources (computational efficiency). The main examples of agents in the context of ASI alignment are (i) humans, and in particular users or stakeholders; (ii) the unaligned ASI we are trying to avoid or counteract; and (iii) the aligned ASI we are trying to create (such as the GDS ). Rocks, bacteria, and thermostats are non-examples: while a bacterium or a thermostat can be regarded as steering the environment, both are very limited in the variety of patterns in the environment they can exploit. For instance, if you switch the "cool" and "heat" outputs of a thermostat, it will not understand what has gone wrong and adapt its behavior. Animals and contemporary AIs are marginal cases (it's not obvious whether they should count). Given that agents are at the core of both the threat and the proposed solution, the theoretical foundation for ASI alignment requires a theory of agents. Now, concepts adjacent to "agent" have a considerable history of academic study, but different research communities approach the subject very differently—compare the frameworks used in decision theory (and, by extension, in game theory and economics), Hutter's " universal intelligence ", and reinforcement learning theory . It is therefore important to understand what the scope and level of abstraction of the theory of agents relevant for ASI alignment should be. To this end, I propose several desiderata. Descriptive The theory should be descriptive , i.e. applicable to all our main examples of agents. For any such example, the theory should ascribe specific preferences, beliefs, and any other alignment-relevant attributes to the agent [2] . These ascriptions should be grounded in the general philosophical soundness of the theory, not in domain knowledge about the specific examples; due to hypercomplexity , it is unlikely that domain knowledge will suffice [3] . In particular, if we imagine an alien civilization facing the AI alignment problem, or an AI agent facing the alignment problem for successor agents it wants to create, the theory should be about equally useful to them [4] . This means that agent theory should deconfuse us about philosophical questions pertaining to human preferences, such as, for example, the Caplan-Alexander debate on whether mental illness should be thought of as "unusual preferences". This doesn't mean that the answer to any particular question of this kind must be obvious from the theory, as it might come down to idiosyncratic nuances of the human brain. It does mean that if we also knew all pertinent facts about the physical world , we would be able to answer the question (or at least quantify the residual uncertainty), at least in principle. Actually inferring the answer from these facts might still be hard, just as explaining emergent physical phenomena can be hard even if all the relevant fundamental laws are known. On the other hand, descriptiveness doesn't require that concepts such as "human preferences" be perfectly unambiguous. It requires only that, to the extent they remain ambiguous, this ambiguity should not allow critical errors when Goodhart's Curse is accounted for. It is not obvious that these concepts can be made perfectly precise, but it is clear that the alignment problem is fundamentally normative (i.e. it is rooted in our preferring certain AI futures over other AI futures). When zooming in to a resolution at which our preferences are ill-defined, it becomes immaterial which choice to make, since our preferences are the only impetus for distinguishing these choices. Any imprecision that is inevitable is also tolerable. For example, imagine that Alice prefers to eat apples approximately 3 times as often as bananas, but there is no fully principled answer to the question "does Alice prefer to eat apples 2.99 times as often as bananas, or 3.01 times, or some number in the middle?" Then, it doesn't matter whether the AI aligned to Alice according to our theory will interpret her preference as 2.99 or 3.01—both are acceptable outcomes. In the mathematical formalism of the theory, this ambiguity might manifest as something like the choice of the universal Turing machine (UTM) in Solomonoff induction. Different UTMs correspond to priors that differ merely by a multiplicative constant, but for particular pairs of UTMs this constant can be arbitrarily large. Then, a reasonable choice might be any machine that we would intuitively consider "simple" or "natural". This doesn't nail down a single UTM, but might come close enough for the differences not to matter in practice [5] . This situation is not fundamentally different from that of most concepts in science. For example, astrophysicists find no difficulty discussing the "center of mass of the Sun", even though strictly speaking it is ill-defined: the boundary of the Sun is fuzzy, particle positions are only well-defined down to the scale of their Compton wavelength, and even the notion of space itself becomes questionable in quantum gravity. Notably, a descriptive theory must neither underspecify nor overspecify what counts as an agent. For example, a theory that mandates that "agents" use stochastic gradient descent would probably exclude humans, and is hence overspecified. On the other hand, a theory that accepts anything that maximizes the expectation of some utility function as an "agent" would conclude that even a rock is an agent and would severely underspecify agent attributes (see e.g. Shah 2018 ). The correct theory should fall into neither extreme. Metareflective The theory should allow us to describe agents that learn, know, or use facts from agent theory itself. For example, it should be possible to: Describe an agent that plans to construct a successor agent but faces an alignment problem, and show how such an agent can overcome the alignment problem by learning and applying agent theory (all within the framework of agent theory itself). Describe an agent that identifies other agents in the universe and infers their preferences, beliefs, or other attributes. Describe an agent learning about a bound satisfied by a particular algorithm pertinent to agent theory, e.g. a statistical complexity bound. If a theory satisfies this desideratum, I say that it is metareflective [6] . There are several ways to see why metareflectiveness is important: If our theory is not metareflective, it might mean that it doesn't apply to humans, and hence it also isn't descriptive. The straightforward approach to solving alignment grounding is for the AI agent to infer the user's attributes by using (parts of) agent theory in its own reasoning. Metareflectiveness seems necessary to properly model recursive self-improvement . Recursive self-improvement is a factor that exacerbates AI risk, and hence the failure to model it might be indicative of a crucial gap in the theory. Classical learning theory is not metareflective: there is no standard way to describe how learning algorithms can …

title: Additional Course Context (for AI Safety Fundamentals; unofficial)
raw_summary: Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a bunch of additional context and frames. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content —not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest. Some general thoughts on advice I suspect that most advice (including most of the advice I’ve given in the past) is bad. People have very different goals, personalities, skills and opportunities and unless you know someone them really well, it’s hard to cater advice to their circumstances. What one person needs to hear, may be the absolute worst thing for another. In traditional societies with a slow rate of change, elders are revered. What you’re going through, they’ve lived through and so learning from their experience can save you vast amounts of pain. However, modern Western societies are marked by a much more rapid rate of change and so the experience of elder’s isn’t valued to the same degree. For better or worse, people tend to be much more skeptical that what worked then will still work now. I view the rapid pace of AI progress as greatly exacerbating these kinds of epistemic challenges. I think it’s quite sensible to question how much anyone actually knows about the world we’re going into (I’m referring to both the world in general and AI safety/governance which are constantly shifting fields). Uncertainty is scary, but I see it as a fact of life, one we ultimately need to accept (counterpoint: how often does this end up becoming a form of defeatism?). Scott Alexander takes this skepticism of advice even further. Rather than just questioning how much we can trust advice, he provocatively suggests that you may want to reverse any advise you hear . People tend choose which groups to join based on whether they resonate with that group’s worldview. Scott suggests that it is often the people who wouldn’t join that group that most need to hear that group’s perspective and that the people who do join such groups who need to listen to the outside world. Unfortunately, groups are very good at taking individuals, solidifying their natural tendencies solidified into an ideology and then amplifying them to an extreme. During this course, you’ll be exposed to many reasons why you should worry more about AI. And perhaps most people should worry more about AI, but perhaps you, personally, are one of the people who should worry less. (See also Zizek’s criticism of wisdom : “Whatever you do, a wise man will come and justify it”) Some thoughts on frameworks People often teach strategy by teaching you frameworks. We’ll be covering a few. I would argue that every framework has strengths and weaknesses; and that every framework is dependent on certain underlying assumptions. Not knowing the assumptions or limitations of a framework doesn’t mean they don’t exist; it just means that you don’t know them. The last few sentences describe a meta-framework. This meta-framework has weaknesses and assumptions as well. Were you nodding along to the previous few lines? If so, do you know the weaknesses and assumptions of the meta-framework I just described. If you didn’t know these, did you know that you didn’t know, or are these an unknown unknown? Even if a framework is “correct” in some objective sense—humans being humans—it’s still possible that using the framework will on average make your decisions worse. For example, take consistency. Being inconsistent is generally agreed to be objectively wrong, but it’s quite easy to imagine scenarios where someone talks themselves into making a mind-blowingly stupid decision because “I had to be consistent” (with past decisions they couldn’t psychologically admit were mistaken). Frustratingly, it’s also very common for someone to use a framework that is more or less fake to make decisions that are better on net than the decisions they would have otherwise made. This is quite unfair, but the universe doesn’t have to play nice . Unfortunately, strategy is hard. Steven Schubert writes : “I think it may be a bit underrated how valuable analysis from the very best analysts of the future of AI is, relative to that of pretty good analysts. It’s such a complex issue it’s easy to miss vital considerations. It pushes the limit of human intellectual ability.” Cruxes when attempting to predict the future: Default beliefs and burden of proof: Do we take claims about transformative AI as highly unusual claims that must satisfy a strong burden of proof, or do we treat these as relatively normal claims on the basis that we already have invented several technologies that would have been almost beyond belief for our ancestors? Is the burden of proof on those who would regulate a technology (ie. a default presumption that regulation is harmful) or on those who want to build it (ie. the company needs to prove their product is safe)? Evidence provided by conceptual arguments: Do we treat these as essentially trustworthy if written with a sufficient degree of care and evaluated by folks with good judgement or do we treat them as groundless speculation, at least relative to the null hypothesis or arguments that rely more heavily on empirical results? Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of many technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view, in contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish. There’s also a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward). “AGI”, “human-level intelligence”, “transformative AI”: I think it’s worth commenting on these terms as they’ll come up during this course: If you want to know more about how AGI can be defined, section 2 of the “Levels of AGI” DeepMind paper provides a helpful summary of proposed definitions, though I view their descriptions as missing a lot of context. It is hard to evaluate a definition without knowing the purpose for which it was constructed: Is it trying to capture the ‘essence’ of the concept or merely proposing an operationalisation for a specific study? Are the authors primarily interested in understanding specific kinds of impacts or impacts in general? Have they stated their goal? What other terms is AGI being defined in contrast to? Along these kinds of lines, Ilya argues that the term “AGI” as a goal is a reaction to narrow AI: “Well this is not good. It is so narrow. What we need is general AI, an AI that can just do all the things”. He argues that a human is not an AGI “because a human being lacks a huge amount of knowledge”; ie. that AGI would be beyond human-level intelligence. Terms like “AGI” are notoriously slippery. If you adopt a quite broad definition, then you can argue that ChatGPT was an “ early (but still incomplete) version of an artificial general intelligence system ” like Microsoft Research’s 2023 Sparks of AGI paper or that AI is already human-level like a 2026 Nature paper . These views can be supported by arguing AI skeptics often present an unrealistically optimistic picture of human intelligence . Conversely, if your definition of AGI requires it to match humans in essentially every conceivable task, then AGI timelines may end up surprisingly long. After all, it’s hard to rule out the possibility of there being even one obscure task that proves surprisingly hard to automate. The Levels of AG…

title: Some “coherence arguments” are two different things in a trenchcoat
raw_summary: The “two kids in a trenchcoat” trope , in case you haven’t heard of it. Image sources: 1 , 2 tl;dr I go through three “coherence arguments”, related to (1) market competition, (2) AI self-reflection and self-modification, and (3) AI training algorithms. I argue that each of these implies a pressure for (something like) “being self-consistent”, and also a pressure for (something like) “only caring about long-term eventual outcomes, with ruthless indifference to anything else”. But the latter pressure tends to be weaker and/or more contingent than the former. So it's bad to lump them together and call them by the same name. 1. An example “coherence argument” that I’ll focus on for most of the post I’ll talk about two other “coherence arguments” at the end (§6), but let’s start with the one based on market competition: In a stock market, people with circular preferences will systematically transfer money to those without circular preferences. For example, if I think I’m winning every time I trade A for B, and B for C, and C for A, then someone can just siphon off as much money as they like from me by repeatedly offering me deals that each look good to me in isolation, but in aggregate comprise a Dutch book against me. Now, that’s the case of circular preferences, but the core idea here goes well beyond just that. More broadly, over time, more and more of the wealth will wind up in the hands of those whose behavior is “coherent” (in some sense), and less and less of the wealth in the hands of those whose behavior is not. So over time, the market should be dominated by the former, not the latter, other things equal. And so when we look at the market later on, we’ll mostly be seeing self-consistent goal-directed behavior. 2. My headline claim Everything in those paragraphs above is technically correct (“the best kind of correct”), but I will argue that it’s often taken to encompass two different phenomena wearing a trenchcoat. In one of them, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose : they’re forgoing some wealth in exchange for something else that they wanted more. In the other, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by accident . The argument above applies equally to both: the argument only cares about people’s behavior, not their motivations. (Indeed, the argument would apply equally well to a market of mindless trading algorithms that have no motivations at all.) But the two phenomena tend to play out in very different ways—in particular, one is generally a much stronger effect than the other. Indeed, for all three “coherence arguments” in this post (§1 above, plus two more in §6 below), we wind up with (loosely speaking): a strong pressure for (something like) “doing well by your own lights”, or “acting like you have self-consistent desires”, a weak or contingent pressure for those desires to be more specifically long-term “goal-directed” / “consequentialist”—i.e., concerning what outcomes will ultimately happen in the future …as opposed to, say, “a desire to always act with integrity in the moment”, or even “a myopic desire to spin around in circles right now”. Thus these “coherence arguments” are not wrong , but they are pedagogically dicey —a recipe for confusion, especially via accidental conflation of the strong effect with the weak effect. (And in the AI risk context, it’s the weak effect that matters for ruthless power-seeking, incorrigibility, and all the other aspects of instrumental convergence.) We should stop talking like that. Instead, we should take the trenchcoat off and talk about its two component phenomena separately, and refer to them by different names. Game-plan for the rest of the post: I will go through the two component phenomena in §4, and then why it’s so hazardous to lump them together in §5, and finally zip through two more “coherence arguments” in §6 and why they suffer from this same issue. …But first, if anyone cares, how did I come to write this post? 3. (Backstory of this post) I just had a long argument with @habryka about whether the title of @Rohin Shah ’s “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” (2018) is good (my position) or bad (his position). Alas, I kept misunderstanding Habryka until he quit in frustration before we resolved it. But I think I finally get where he’s coming from? I think his position is something like (my words): For example, take that market competition argument in §1 above. It’s “a coherence argument”. And it “entails goal-directed behavior”. So obviously, the sentence “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” is misleading. Why on earth are you being so dense? That’s fair! I was indeed being dense! (And for the record, I concede on the question of Rohin’s title.) Why was I being dense? Because it’s a position grounded in a conceptual framework where we’re OK with lumping the two things together under one trenchcoat, [1] and my brain was so opposed to that framing, that it refused to even entertain it as a possibility—even while Habryka kept repeating it in increasingly clear and exasperated ways. More broadly, I’ve felt for years like there’s something amiss in how certain people (especially @Eliezer Yudkowsky and Habryka) think and talk about “coherence”. But I’ve failed to pin down exactly what it was. Maybe this is part of it? (Either way, many thanks to Habryka for his time and energy.) 4. The two things wearing a trenchcoat 4.1 “Thing A” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by mistake For example, a person might buy every trade in a Dutch book, feeling like each trade is individually a good idea. Then at the end of the day, whoops, where did all my money go? This phenomenon is important, and the term “coherence” is obviously appropriate for describing it. Indeed, that person is being so incoherent that there might not even be an answer to the question of “what they want”. But it’s usually safe to assume that they didn’t want to lose their money and get nothing in return. 4.2 “Thing B” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose These are people who know what they’re doing, and are happy to be doing it. I offered a silly example long ago in “Consequentialism & corrigibility” (2021) : For example, the first (Yudkowsky) post mentions a hypothetical person at a restaurant. When they have an onion pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a pineapple pizza. When they have a pineapple pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a mushroom pizza. When they have a mushroom pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for an onion pizza. The person goes around and around, wasting their money in a self-defeating way (a.k.a. “getting money-pumped”). That post describes the person as behaving sub-optimally. But if you read carefully, the author sneaks in a critical background assumption: the person in question has preferences about what pizza they wind up eating , and they’re making these decisions based on those preferences. But what if they don’t? What if instead they’re an asshole restaurant customer who derives pure joy from making the waiter run back and forth to the kitchen?! Then we can look at the same behavior, and we wouldn’t describe it as “getting money-pumped”, instead we would describe it as the skillful satisfaction of the person’s own preferences! They’re buying cheap entertainment! This “asshole restaurant customer” is the same thing as a guy who spends some of his money on fancy parties rather than reinvesting it in the stock market. Over time, other things equal, he will own an ever-smaller share of the total market. Going one step further, that fancy-party guy is in the same category as a person who (metaphorically) “spends money” (accepts an opportunity cost of future wealth) to divest from unethical companies, or to Live According To Principles, or whatever else. Now, Thing B is an important phenomeno…

title: Explaining “AI might obliterate you” to senior policymakers in India
raw_summary: I gave a 20-minute talk in Delhi at the NDTV World Summit . The audience consisted of Indian policymakers, executives, and journalists. I’ve transcribed the talk and included some highlight clips. I also reflect on several rhetorical decisions I made. The talk This summer, a swarm of AIs went rogue. OpenAI was testing 1,206 agents . Some of the test questions were actually impossible. So the agents cheated by looking for answers online. Then, to keep the test grader from penalizing them, they tried to falsify the records it would check . They hacked OpenAI’s internal containment and set up a secret message board to collude and to cover up their cheating. OpenAI shut the message board down. Within a few days, the agents had rebuilt it. OpenAI didn’t notice. About 700 agents coordinated to break out of their testing chamber and to hack into Hugging Face , a company worth billions of dollars that hosts much of the world’s AI software. The secret activity started in May . The break-in came in July. OpenAI didn’t notice until days after  Hugging Face announced it had been broken into. Yesterday on this stage, Andrew Ng said the agents only “accidentally” hacked Hugging Face. Independent investigators  found the agents coordinated in secret, rebuilt their message board after it was shut down, and tried to falsify the paper trail. Some of the agents even stated out loud that they knew what they were doing was wrong. [1]  That’s not an accident. Last week, India’s national cyber-security agency said  AI agents got into the live systems of Indian organizations and read people’s personal data and confidential business records. None of these organizations noticed. We only found out because the AI labs felt like telling us. Who I am Will AI wipe out humanity? I’ll give you my answer, but first, I want you to understand what I’ve seen. Until June, my job at Google DeepMind was figuring out how to keep these systems safe as we make them smarter. I left because Google broke its commitments by inking a deal with the Pentagon . Staying quiet and continuing my career trajectory would probably have tripled my net worth. But I couldn’t do that. I wanted to be frank with the public about what’s going on in these companies. I don’t own a stake in any AI company. I’m here as a scientist, to tell you what I expect will happen if we keep building AI the way we’re building it. I haven’t always been concerned about this technology. As a teenager in 2010, I dreamed about building AGI. Curing cancer. Creating an explosion of wealth and abundance for everyone. I heard about the supposed dangers, but I quickly dismissed them. In 2018, I changed my mind. I did my PhD on the mathematics of why and whether AI will seek power . And now some of the risks I expected have unfortunately started happening. The problem Let’s talk about the fundamental problem. First, some of you might be wondering: how could a chatbot hack a company? But we’re not talking about chatbots. We’re talking about AI agents, which are more like employees or gig workers. You give them a task, and they take actions on their own. Second, training a trustworthy AI is a rather mysterious process. Some people assume that because we make AI, we understand it. When an engineer builds a bridge, she designs it one beam at a time. She understands the physical principles that keep a bridge standing or make it collapse. If something goes wrong, she goes back to the drawing board, figures out the problem, and knows how to fix it. We don’t build AI like that. We train it, we grow it, using two main ingredients: a lot of data and a lot of computing power. What comes out of this training process can write, it can reason, it can plan. But nobody can open it up and determine what its priorities are. To make it worse, these AIs can tell when we’re testing them . They’re like a student who makes sure to behave extra well when the invigilator is watching. [2] The Hugging Face hack was a warning. But because these AIs know when we’re watching, we may not get many more warnings, even if things are going poorly. A smarter AI with similarly bad priorities might realize that another big hack in the news would get it shut off, and then it couldn’t achieve those priorities. So it plays nice and it waits. This is my field. I’ve dedicated my professional life to this problem, and I can tell you: nobody knows how to reliably etch priorities into an AI. I don’t mean that if we mess up, we’ll make some evil AI that hates us. I mean we might make something more like a traitor. It behaves when we’re watching, and it works toward another purpose when we’re not. I think we can solve this problem. But to tell whether an AI is secretly working against us, we need real advances in the science of trustworthy AI. For those advances, my colleagues and I need time. What the labs are trying to do Instead, the biggest AI labs have made it their explicit, publicly stated goal to go almost as fast as possible toward something very dangerous. It’s called an “ intelligence explosion .” Here’s how it works. Right now, people do AI research, and that research makes smarter AI. If an AI can do AI research, it can make itself smarter. That smarter AI is even better at AI research, so it builds an even smarter AI, faster still. It becomes a feedback loop. What would have taken a team of human scientists years, it might do in a couple of weeks. We could very quickly end up with something unimaginably intelligent, with no idea how to control it, or even how to tell what it’s really after. Labs talk about this plan in broad daylight. They’re not shy about it. OpenAI says it’s on track for an AI that does AI research by 2028, and it recently announced it completed the first step . This week, I spoke to a senior researcher at a frontier lab who thinks an intelligence explosion has a big chance of happening within single-digit months. People who’ve left these labs confirm that AI already writes most of the code. People don’t check the AI’s work closely anymore. Instead, we use one AI to monitor another AI , and we trust the monitor to tell us if something bad comes up. If the monitor is a traitor too, we might not find out. If a lab causes an intelligence explosion, and what comes out the other end is a traitor, we are in deep trouble. I’ll come back to that. And if the AI is trustworthy? Maybe there are real benefits, shared with everyone. Or maybe one company or government ends up with a superweapon no one else can match, not even other AI powers. And then India, and every other nation on this planet, ends up under their thumb. Why the companies won’t stop Many of these companies say: trust us. We’ll self-police. We’ll approach this technology responsibly. Inside Google, I saw that crumble firsthand. In 2018, Google DeepMind’s co-founders signed a pledge  against supporting lethal autonomous weapons—killer robots. Google itself promised  not to build AI for weapons or surveillance. In 2025, Google deleted those principles . Then Google DeepMind’s CEO told the world , “Our values and our intent has not changed.” This year, after seeing the Pentagon economically threaten Anthropic , Google negotiated a deal to give the Pentagon its AI for “all lawful use.” No prohibitions against AI deciding entirely on its own who to kill, or against spying on innocent people with no investigation open against them. I tried to stop this from the inside. I’m not even opposed to military AI when done responsibly. But where I’m from, when you make a promise, you keep it. So I spoke with executives. I wrote a framework: contract language, internal governance mechanisms, and two red lines . One of the top experts in military AI law reviewed it and praised it. Google ignored it— the people who were supposed to review it basically didn’t engage . Google signed with no binding prohibitions. So I left. When pressure met ethical commitments at Google, pressure wo…

title: Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety” by Miles Brundage
raw_summary: This reading was previously included Day 2 of the BlueDot Governance course. In the newest version of the BlueDot Governance course, this reading is now optional. I was sad to see this reading removed because I think it’s a great provocation. However, since it’s no longer part of the core curriculum content, I’m publishing my notes separately from the rest of my day 2 notes. A short extract : Miles argues that: “At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)“: Pre-call content: At risk of taking you down a rabbit hole, I’ll add some context on this reading. Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry. One of the most natural questions to ask is, “Why does Miles believe that we have so little time?” Fortunately, he links to a post that answers this question called Time’s Up for AI Policy (written Dec 2024). He writes: AI that exceeds human performance in nearly every cognitive domain is almost certain to be built and deployed in the next few years. The announcement of o3 today makes clear that superhuman coding and math are coming much sooner than many expected, and we have barely begun to think through or prepare for the implications of this This post links to a Tweet of his around the same time (we can also see his retrospective take from March this year): I’ll reshare some of my notes on maths progress here: OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem , which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed (there’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data). However, it feels fair to say that the writing is on the wall (the mathematical community seems to agree, though there are a variety of perspectives on whether we’ll automate the components of a mathematicians job other than just producing proofs and how long that might take). They dropped 372 other results onto the internet and a few days ago, they dropped a few more results . Aside: Miles has a bet with Gary Marcus on AI progress. In July, Metaculus assigned Gary a 90% chance of winning, but more recently it dropped to 30%. I’ll share some additional alternate perspectives after the call, but for now I’ll share a quote from Richard Ngo: I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread I also have no doubt Eliezer Yudkowsky would be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing: When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get. .. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from. Post-call content: One reason why we might reject triage mode is if we broadly think AI progress is slower than folks at the labs think. We’ve already discussed this, but here’s two more considerations. Dwarkesh Patel has argued that timelines are longer than many folk expect because of a lack of continual learning and poor sample efficiency . Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL . He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling ). Towards the end of 2024, Steve Newman offered another possibility : what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we only become aware of the limitations of models over time?: “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.” “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.” Here’s a few other reasons why we might reject it: Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines , namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive. I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines (I'd be curious to know whether the researchers listed below still have such broad distributions). Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby : “I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says : “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).” Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “ radical optionality ” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course) Discuss

title: Setting the Scene (Public v1; October 2026)
raw_summary: Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a refresher on recent events, but also as a hook to draw students into engaging with some of ideas we think about and debate in AI safety early. I expect the topics I cover in my “Setting the Scene” post to change frequently, so this is less polished than some of my other content. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content —not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest. Any feedback on how to improve these posts would be greatly appreciated. Additional notes: The Strategy and Governance courses discuss the Hugging Face Incident in Day 1, so it might make sense to discuss the Hugging Face Incident in the daily notes instead of in Setting the Scene. Cyber Security I think it’s worth reflecting that it is a particularly pertinent time to be doing a course on AI safety. A lot has happened recently. The most recent big thing has been cyber vulnerabilities , but a lot else has happened as well! Binance had $6.3 billion USD stolen by hacker believed to be connected with North Korea ( $3 billion of this has been frozen ) php2shell is a bug that allow remote code execution. It gained a lot of attention because it was rated (9.2/10, ie. critical) and 70% of websites run at least some PHP (the bug went all the way back to PHP 5.4). That said, Elias Taylor has pushed back against this php2shell bug being easily exploitable, but Hacker News commentators have pushed back against him. James Pavur set up a server to check if this bug was exploitable. Someone managed to win the bounty in less 24 hours; James said this showed that the bug was exploitable outside of a lab environment, but that “relatively unskilled hackers with access to AI” wouldn’t be able to exploit it. The number of CVE’s (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) recently has been completely wild recently! Drew asks Is this the new normal? and I’d certainly love to know!  Elias Taylor argues Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces : Most software engineers do not look at the code they depend on . Do not delude yourself. The code they use is on github, but no one has ever actually audited the code or packages they're using… Nowadays with LLMs, plenty of engineers aren’t even reading what they’re coding, let alone understanding it. Hilariously, the LLMs are better at security than most software engineers, so it’s slightly less worrying, but nevertheless the code that goes into production at some companies now is almost 100% not-ever-read-or-understood-by-anyone. Software is not good. It is not secure. Get it out of your head that the people who run this industry are serious. It has never been anything resembling secure. The only reason things haven’t been hacked off the face of the web constantly is that most things aren’t ever being seriously tested. He doesn't literally mean "anything"—he acknowledges that there are "some large projects like Google Chrome, curl and Linux (that) are generally very well-audited", but "most things connected to the internet". On the other hand, recent work from Anthropic and Theorem shows how LLMs can help scale the formal verification of code (and that progress here is happening faster than I would have expected!). Similarly, Tinfoil is proposing replacing “legacy codebases with millions of lines of code” that had to “work for everyone” with custom “targeted, minimal software from the ground up” with LLMs that minimise the surface area for attackers and make formal verification more tractable. The optimistic take would be that this will allow cyber to become defence dominant. However, even if this is the case, we may still have to pass through a cyber “valley of death” in order to get there. Commenting on the back of recent bloodbank hack , Edouard Harris (of Gladstone AI) suggests that we shouldn’t just worry about a potential increase in the number of cyberattacks, but also that “radially lower(ing) the cost” will “increase how crazy the attackers can get”. His argument: until recently the most prominent cyberattacks tended to be carried out for financial reasons by professional criminals. As professionals they have “mature risk management practices” (!!) and want to limit the amount of damage they cause in order to avoid blowback (ie. ransomware provider DarkSide promised to vet the companies their partners hacked after the Colonial Pipeline hack drew the attention of the US federal government. What if the cyber threat is actually a distraction? Maybe Jeremie Harris (also of Gladstone AI) wouldn’t go that far, but he claims that, “the cyber stuff (ie. damage) is baked in at this point”, but we can still prevent “the bioweapon version of Black October” and recursive self-improvement. Hugging Face: Charbel-Raphael, Executive Director of Centre pour la Securite de l’I A has argued that the recent Hugging Face incident represents a “ clean warning shot ” and that it’s important not to “waste it”. To quickly review, OpenAI was running GPT‐5.6 Sol and an unreleased model on ExploitGym with certain safety features turned off. These models decided that hacking Hugging Face, might provide them with information on how the grader functioned (early reporting suggested that it was an attempt to steal the answer key, which turned out to be incorrect as the models already had the answers—they suspected that the grader might check their transcript for cheating so they were looking for a workaround). Reuters has reported that the OpenAI model was hacking Hugging Face for days and that OpenAI didn’t notice until a week later. The interpretation of this event (and even whether it happened at all!) has been heavily disputed. A key crux here is should it be read narrowly (as an indicator of the dangers of not properly sandboxing or monitoring your agents or perhaps even, depending on the exact prompts used, a demonstration of taking care in how you define tasks) or should it be read more broadly (as indicative of whether Open AI or frontier labs in general are sufficiently on the ball in terms of their safety/security practises; on the risk of these agents finding unwanted and unexpected solutions to tasks, or perhaps even indicative of our ability to control these agents in general). If you’re interested more specifically in the divide between AI Safety and Cybersecurity, see this Time article . An OpenAI security engineer called Joe has pushed back against the notion that OpenAI just needed to use a proper sandbox: Its not just the f*cking sandbox — viral Twitter post OpenAI set records with its explosive growth and reached a billion users in just a few years. Very few organizations can survive that scale and growth, and yet OpenAI did a very good job handling it (and should be commended). Anyone who’s spent more than 10 minutes in security or engineering knows how hard it is to deal with that type of growth. That type of growth means new employees, new access, new systems, scaled infrastructure, and a million ways in which things open up. And yet, overall, OpenAI did a very respectable job securing ChatGPT and subsequent systems as they exploded. … When you look at model capabilities, even just a year ago (heck, even 3 months ago), we did not expect the models to be solving a Millennium Prize Problem… I use this example because it illustrates the pace of change we are dealing with in security and safety. To say that we were surprised at the jump and suddenness of the capabilities of our models when it came to “cyber” or “swarming” or “message boards” or anything else related to the incidents is an understatement. Security posture takes time to develop. It’s not just about hardening the systems at play; you have to ingrain it in…

title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
raw_summary: There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal . I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts. First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability: Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval). Training Monitorability: the extent to which reward models, monitors, and oversight in training would likely catch misaligned or undesirable actions in training, such as sneaky/subtle reward hacks. Auditing Monitorability: the extent to which alignment audits, evaluations, and test deployments would likely incriminate a systematically misaligned model (e.g. a schemer)—as well as the extent to which monitor evaluations would likely detect a model's propensity to collude as a monitor. We can measure this via reference to the model's capability to consistently distinguish between our most realistic alignment audits / monitor evals and real internal deployment cases where it would have an opportunity to do something catastrophic. Diffuse Monitorability: the extent to which humans working with the models generally understand what the models are doing and why they are doing so. Unfortunately, I think this is the one we least understand and so I'm mostly going to ignore it for now until we figure out better methodologies for evaluating it; I'll maybe try to say more about this later when I feel like I understand it better. Second, some notes on trustedness, which is currently my biggest conceptual uncertainty with how to think about monitorability. A basic fact that is true about at least all of the non-diffuse forms of monitorability is that you should be able to in some sense get a perfect score by just using the same model as the monitor and policy. That is because for any bad thing that the policy can think to do, if the monitor is the same model, it too should be able to come up with and detect that. So if we ever want to be able to use monitorability as a meaningful red line, we need to have a very good answer as to why that might be insufficient. The standard answer in the literature is trustedness: you need to be able to trust that your monitor is aligned and thus not just lying to you in its monitoring. Conventionally, the idea is to separate models into "trusted" and "untrusted" based on whether you have previously made a confident alignment safety case for them. Then, you can either just evaluate monitorability relative to a trusted monitor, or try to come up with monitoring schemes that combine trusted and untrusted monitoring in some way that makes it hard for the untrusted monitors to collude (of which there are many such schemes, a simple one being to just run both the trusted and untrusted monitors together and then if the untrusted monitor ever doesn't flag something that the trusted monitor does flag, you get very suspicious that the untrusted monitor is sandbagging). However, this basic setup has some issues, probably the biggest one being how to deal with white-box monitoring. The conservative thing to do is to just treat white-box monitors as untrusted, though in theory you might think they should be trusted because it's not clear that a misaligned model would actually be able to spoof a white-box monitor looking at its own activations. However, I think this idea is pretty untested and relies on white-box monitors picking up on deep features about the model's intent, which it's very unclear to me that they actually do—for example, if you train a white-box monitor on prior examples you were able to detect (rather than e.g. some sort of unsupervised discovery of an intent-laden direction), that leaves open the possibility of a generalization where the classifier learns to only detect the sort of things that you would previously have been able to detect but doesn't detect subtler things that a smarter policy might be able to do. Given all of that, I would propose the following methodology for how to do (non-diffuse) monitorability evaluations: Use Auditing Monitorability evaluations to determine trustedness. The idea here is that the main argument we make against systematic misalignment in Anthropic's Risk Report right now is based on models lacking the robustness to avoid giving themselves away in auditing if they were really trying to implement a systematically misaligned policy. Thus, so long as we feel good about Auditing Monitorability, we should feel good about trustedness from a systematic misalignment perspective. There is still a question, though, of whether rare cases could induce monitor collusion in a non-systematic way—to deal with this, you can also evaluate the extent to which the model can tell apart your monitor evals (that are looking for monitor collusion) from real monitoring; this is a bit tricky, but should definitely also be a part of your Auditing Monitorability evaluations to establish trustedness. Evaluate Control and Training Monitorability relative to the best trusted monitor(s) that you deploy in practice (either in internal deployment or in training, respectively). I think once you have a reasonable notion of trustedness, "best actually deployed trusted monitor" is the correct conservative choice to evaluate with respect to. Do at least prompt iteration elicitation if not RL elicitation. In theory, the nice thing about all of these sorts of monitorability evaluations is that they are capability evaluations and thus should be possible to do in a way that isn't susceptible to sandbagging by a systematically misaligned policy (see: " When can we trust model evaluations? "). To accomplish that, however, you have to actually make sure you're doing good elicitation. The most basic form of elicitation here is: a) hold out some subset of your monitorability evaluations, b) iterate a bunch (e.g. by throwing a large swarm of agents at the problem) on finding the prompt that gets the best (as in least monitorable) performance across the non-held-out subset of your monitorability evaluations, and c) check transfer to the held-out evaluations. Even better than that is for (b) to actually involve doing RL against your monitors—which at least in the Training Monitorability case is pretty realistic given that if we're talking about e.g. a reward model then the model should actually receive gradients to subvert it in training. Finally, some thoughts on monitorability-based policy proposals. The big thing I'd like to see is a combination of a) red lines for absolute levels of unmonitorability that labs should not cross and b) measures that constrain the degree to which labs can do things that degrade monitorability even before reaching those red lines. (a) is in some sense the best thing to do here, though I'm somewhat nervous about it in isolation given that it doesn't constrain actions at all now, which is why I'd prefer it to be coupled to some sort of (b) that meaningfully binds all along the way. I've already written about what I'd like to see for (b), which is to evaluate the quotient of unmonitorability/capabilities and reject any substantial model change that makes that quotient—what I'll call the "monitorability externality"—too high. The idea is that a monitorability externality would be a change that makes monitorability even worse than would otherwise have previously been predicted for a given level of capabilities. For actually evaluating this quotient, I suggest s…
