title: Advancing safe agentic AI: ASKS symposium highlights
raw_summary: Highlights from UIUC’s 2026 ASKS Fall Symposium. On September 24–25, academic researchers, enterprise scientists and leaders gathered at the Thomas M. Siebel Center for Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) for the ASKS Fall Symposium. The event marked a major milestone in the partnership between Capital One and the University of Illinois through the Capital One Center for Generative AI Safety, Knowledge Systems and Cybersecurity (ASKS). Designed to advance the safety, reliability and security of generative AI models, the symposium featured keynotes, research readouts, panel debates and a hands-on AI red-teaming workshop. From models to agents: Navigating the age of action The symposium kicked off with opening remarks and a fireside chat titled “From models to agents: rethinking AI research, safety, and cybersecurity in the age of action.” Moderated by ASKS Co-Director Heng Ji, the session featured Prem Natarajan, chief scientist and chief enterprise AI officer at Capital One, alongside Nancy Amato, director of the Siebel School of Computing and Data Science. The discussion framed the fundamental transition taking place across the AI landscape: moving away from models that merely generate text to autonomous agentic AI-systems that can set goals, execute code, operate tools and take multistep actions. Natarajan highlighted Capital One’s “destination-back” scientific approach, emphasizing that in highly regulated spaces like financial services, autonomous agency requires rigorous safety mechanisms. As AI stops just “talking” and starts “acting,” industry-academic partnerships like ASKS become essential to build new sandboxing, auditing and accountability frameworks. Panel spotlight: Word models vs. world models One of the highlights of the day was a panel exploring the fundamental limits of current large language models: “ Word models vs. world models: Do LLMs understand the world-or just describe it? ” Moderated by Heng Ji, the panel brought together UIUC faculty members Gang Wang, Julia Hockenmaier, Chengxiang Zhai and Katie Driggs-Campbell alongside Capital One AI leaders Sambit Sahu and Yue (Rex) Wu. The panelists debated whether modern foundation models genuinely comprehend real-world dynamics or simply replicate statistical language patterns. The consensus pointed toward a need for multimodal visual grounding, physical intelligence and trace-aware reasoning to move models from passive text descriptions to true situation understanding. Pioneering research readouts Throughout the symposium, awarded faculty members and doctoral fellows presented breakthrough findings from ASKS-funded research projects spanning safety, code reasoning and cybersecurity: LLM reasoning and faithfulness: Hao Peng presented work on advancing reasoning faithfulness without explicit rewards, while Talia Ringer’s team introduced TrACE-Contrast for faithful code reasoning. Yuxiong Wang presented work on building safe and trustworthy LLM-based agents by addressing key challenges in evaluation, privacy preservation and multi-agent coordination. Guaranteed safety for agentic AI: Sasa Misailovic detailed SafeAgency , a framework designed to guarantee safety in agentic workflows, complemented by Katherine Driggs-Campbell’s analysis of failures in agentic systems. Security and cybersecurity benchmarks: Bo Li’s team showcased Sentinel Agent for secure agentic architectures, Varun Chandrasekaran’s team presented insights into pragmatic LLM jailbreaking and Daniel Kang introduced CVE-Bench++ , a benchmark for evaluating AI agents in cybersecurity contexts. Keynote on code generation safety: ASKS Director Gang Wang delivered a keynote on automated red-teaming and reasoning to secure code generation models. Doctoral fellow spotlights: Emerging researchers Hyeonjeong Ha, Jeonghwan Kim, Yizhuo Chen, Cheng Qian and Chenyuan Yang presented research on perceptual grounding, data sanitization and physical intelligence. The afternoon program highlighted Capital One’s research initiatives during a session chaired by Sambit Sahu, featuring lightning talks by senior research directors Kartik Balasubramaniam, Genta Winata and Stephen Rawls on scalable AI foundations and system architecture. Red-teaming workshop On the second day of the event, domain specialists convened for a smaller, more intimate AI red-teaming workshop. Alexandre Day (Capital One), Sriram Venkatapathy (Capital One), Varun Chandrasekaran (UIUC) and Gang Wang (UIUC) organized technical talks and working group sessions across three primary focus areas: Novel and diversity-driven red-teaming: Led by Capital One’s Sriram Venkatapathy, the session examined how financial AI systems must adhere to strict multilayered policy frameworks-spanning federal regulations (e.g., FCRA, UDAP), enterprise governance and application-specific constraints. Discussions highlighted that evaluating enterprise safety requires detecting policy omissions (such as missing mandatory disclosures or consent prompts) as well as defending against strategy-conditioned jailbreaks, chain-of-thought forgery and loopholes in complex policy specifications. Red-teaming multi-agent systems: Led by Gang Wang, this track focused on security vulnerabilities unique to multi-agent architectures. Researchers analyzed risks such as indirect prompt injection across workspace topologies, lateral attack propagation between trusted agents, execution-level coordination failures (e.g., data races and deadlocks) and communication-layer enforcement via protocols like NLIP. Evaluation of red-teaming and LLM judges: Led by Rikhiya Ghosh, participants tackled the open challenges of scientifically evaluating safety across long-horizon, multiturn interactions. The group audited LLM-as-a-judge frameworks using semantic factorization (MoE judges), probed reasoning traces for stealthy deception and monitorability failures and explored methods to prevent benchmark contamination through dynamic case generation. Fostering the frontier of talent and research The partnership between Capital One and UIUC continues to drive technical innovation while training the next generation of scientific talent. Highlighting joint breakthroughs like MEMGUARD-a defense mechanism preventing memory contamination in LLMs-the ASKS Center demonstrates the power of combining academic exploration with industrial scale. Capital One looks forward to continuing this strategic collaboration, advancing research in agentic AI and building systems that remain secure, trustworthy and beneficial at scale. Originally published at https://capitalone.science . Advancing safe agentic AI: ASKS symposium highlights was originally published in Capital One Tech on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Capital One at EMNLP 2026 in Budapest
raw_summary: Capital One researchers and academic partners present 16 accepted papers advancing responsible AI, RAG and LLM evaluation. Advancing natural language processing through multi-sector research Natural language processing (NLP) forms the backbone of modern agentic systems, document intelligence and enterprise artificial intelligence applications. Capital One researchers, in collaboration with our academic partners, are presenting 16 accepted papers at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026), taking place in Budapest, Hungary, October 24–29. These research papers highlight ongoing investments in foundational AI/ML science, robust red-teaming, graph-encoded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), intent resolution and trustworthy evaluation techniques. Multi-sector collaboration accelerates the transition of foundational NLP innovations into secure, reliable enterprise systems. By co-authoring several of these papers with university partners including the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Southern California and UNC Chapel Hill, Capital One contributes to open science while addressing complex technical challenges at scale. Highlighted EMNLP 2026 research papers Papers on robustness, red-teaming and model safety: FinRT: Distilling adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators in consumer finance Rikhiya Ghosh, Himanshu Kumar, Sriram Venkatapathy, Sahil Wadhwa, Alexandre Day, Andy Luo, Pranab Mohanty Large language models remain susceptible to adversarial prompts that induce policy-violating behavior in regulated financial contexts. This work introduces FinRT, a framework that distills adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators, significantly improving attack detection and safety verification under fixed generation budgets. MEMGUARD: Preventing memory contamination in long-term memory-augmented large language models Hyeonjeong Ha, William Campbell, Yue Wu (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Long-term memory integration introduces risks of memory contamination in conversational agents. The authors present MEMGUARD, a defense system designed to inspect, isolate and neutralize untrusted external inputs before they corrupt long-term memory stores. Validity-aware jailbreak evaluation for large language models Qilong Wu, Sahil Wadhwa, Pranab Mohanty, Giri Iyengar (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Standard jailbreak evaluations frequently misclassify unviable prompts as successful security breaches. This paper establishes a validity-aware benchmark framework that rigorously validates execution success to ensure accurate safety measurements across frontier language models. Papers on advanced retrieval, graph encoding and intent resolution: CAGE: Coherence-aware graph encoding for retrieval-augmented generation Tong Qi, Jingyu Wu, Youbing Yin, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Traditional vector-based retrieval systems often retrieve relevant to query but collectively incoherent text chunks. CAGE introduces a graph-encoding framework that structures retrieved passages into directed heterogeneous graphs to preserve context relevance, factual consistency and cross-chunk coherence. SPARC-RAG: Adaptive sequential–parallel scaling with context management for retrieval-augmented generation Yuxin Yang, Nima Chitsazan, Yash Govilkar, Akasha Tigalappanavara, Sambit Sahu, Shixiong Zhang (academic partnership with University of Southern California) Naive inference-time scaling in RAG causes context contamination and diminishing returns during complex reasoning. SPARC-RAG coordinates sequential refinement and parallel exploration via unified context management, improving accuracy at lower inference cost. Probing ambiguity: Adversarial intent resolution for robust text-to-SQL Youbing Yin, Xujun Peng, Muhammad Uddin, Erin Babinsky, Daben Liu, Anoop Kumar Natural language database queries frequently contain implicit ambiguities that yield multiple SQL query translations. This paper presents Adversarial Intent Resolution (AIR), a multi-agent framework that actively probes for ambiguity, verifies execution differences and generates targeted clarification. The framework remains effective even when only the database schema, not the underlying data is exposed to the LLM. Papers on LLM evaluation, debiasing and benchmarking: The judge can debias itself: Awareness and self debiasing for reliable LLM-as-a-judge Youbing Yin, Jingyu Wu, Anoop Kumar, Scott Novotney, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Automated LLM-as-a-judge frameworks inherit systematic biases when evaluating output quality. The researchers introduce new benchmarks for additional bias types and demonstrate that self-debiasing strategies can effectively help detect and calibrate their own biases. T1-Bench: Benchmarking multi-scenario agents in large-scale real-world domains Genta Indra Winata, Amartya Chakraborty, Yuzhen Lin, Swasthi Prasannakumarrao, Shikhhar Siingh, Nadia Bathaee, Sriharsha Hatwar, Houhan Lu, Anmol Jain, Paresh Dashore, Anirban Das, Kshitij Tayal, Xiuzhu Lin, Sambit Sahu, Milind Naphade, Shixiong Zhang Evaluating AI agents across diverse industrial tasks requires benchmarks that reflect operational complexity. T1-Bench offers a standardized, multi-scenario benchmarking environment designed to measure multi-step agent reasoning, tool execution and error recovery in real-world workflows. RECAP: Regression evaluation for continual adaptation of prompts Harsh Deshpande, Kushal Chawla, William Campbell Deploying instruction-following models into dynamic environments exposes them to changing constraints. RECAP measures prompt regression, forgetting and forward transfer when constraint specifications evolve over time, offering new metrics for prompt optimization algorithms. Papers on optimization, vision-grounded agents and software engineering: Beyond the vacuum: Combinatorial strategy selection for competitor-aware generative engine optimization Vaibhav Sourirajan, Yao Zhang, Himanshu Kumar, Sahil Wadhwa, Mann Patel, Amirfarrokh Iranitalab Content rewriting strategies in generative engine optimization often operate in isolation without considering competitive market dynamics. This paper introduces a two-phase optimization pipeline using Bayesian Optimization of Combinatorial Structures (BOCS) and preference optimization to learn optimal content rewriting strategies. A history-aware visually grounded critic for computer use agents Jaewoo Lee, Supriyo Chakraborty, Kartik Balasubramaniam, Sambit Sahu (academic partnership with UNC Chapel Hill) Long-horizon GUI agents struggle recovering from errors. This research introduces a test-time intervention framework HiViG which equips the agent with a goal progress oriented summary to produce better actions. The agent then critiques those actions with visually grounded reasoning to refine them. Across a diverse set of GUI environments , HiViG improves task success rates for open-weight and Gemini-3 Flash models by 5.8% and 9.0% relative to the strongest critics evaluated. AREAs-Lab: An interactive environment for AI-driven requirement elicitation for AI systems Pengshan Cai, Sangwoo Cho, Chenyang Zhu, Kushal Chawla, Scott Novotney, Shixiong Zhang, Sambit Sahu (external collaboration with academic and industry partners) Defining precise software and system requirements for AI implementations remains a manual, error-prone task. AREAs-Lab provides an interactive environment that uses LLM agents to elicit, analyze and refine technical requirements prior to system development. VerTox: Verifiable reward-guided corpus poisoning against neural ranking models Zhiqi Huang, Vivek Datla, Alfy Samuel Neural ranking systems in search architectures are susceptible to corpus manipulation. VerTox establishes a verifiable reward-guided evaluation framework to test neural rankers against sophisticated corpus poisoning vectors. Pin…

title: FCA acts to protect consumers facing demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments
raw_summary: We've intervened and Ethica Resolve Limited (Ethica), an FCA authorised firm that services and collects debt on behalf of creditors, has agreed to restrictions. These follow demands it made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. Ethica is acting on behalf of West 28th Street Limited (West 28), which bought disguised remuneration loans from a third party. West 28 is not authorised or regulated by the FCA.Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries. HMRC has published guidance for those affected.Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they're unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.Under the requirements we’ve agreed, Ethica:Will write to affected consumers, explaining that they do not have an enforceable obligation to make payment at this stage. (This means they do not need to pay now while regulatory and legal issues relating to the purported loans are resolved.)Will not make further demands for payment from affected consumers in the current proposed court claim while regulatory and legal issues are resolved.Additionally, Ethica and West 28 will not ask a court to make a judgment against someone who has not responded to a legal claim. This is known as a ‘default judgment’. However, consumers should not ignore any formal court documents they receive on this issue. They should consider seeking independent legal or debt advice before deciding what to do.Additional protections for vulnerable consumers are being put in place and Ethica will identify affected consumers who may be vulnerable.It has not yet been decided whether the debts can be enforced, which may be decided by a court. The requirements agreed protect consumers from avoidable harm while the relevant regulatory and legal issues are resolved. Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

title: Looking back to move forward: why reviewing our rules matters
raw_summary: Markets evolve. Consumer behaviour changes. Technology creates new opportunities and risks. Rules that were appropriate when they were introduced may need to be updated, simplified or, in some cases, removed altogether.That is why the FCA regularly reviews its rules.

title: FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime
raw_summary: A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing. The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.Notes to editorsRead more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: Act now to be resilient in the quantum future
raw_summary: Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.What firms need to do nowSo, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to:Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.How we are supporting firmsWe are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.You can find more information:NCSC, Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptographyG7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sectorCMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

title: New FCA rules bring ESG rating providers into UK regulation for the first time
raw_summary: New UK rules for environmental, social and governance (ESG) rating providers will raise standards in the market, helping investors to make better informed decisions. The new framework brings ESG rating providers into FCA regulation for the first time, covering a market that plays an important role in investment decisions. The rules are designed to improve the transparency, reliability and comparability of ESG ratings, helping build confidence in the information investors rely on. The regime applies to firms or organisations providing ESG ratings and assessments to ensure reliability across the market. The FCA has published guidance to help firms understand whether they may be in scope. Laura Dawes, director of authorisations and sustainable finance at the FCA, said: 'Trusted information is essential for well-functioning markets. These rules will help improve transparency and raise standards across the ESG ratings market while supporting competition, innovation and growth. 'Firms should check now whether they are in scope and start preparing for authorisation. We'll continue to provide practical support to help them prepare.'The new framework introduces requirements covering transparency, governance, systems and controls, the management of conflicts of interest, and engagement with users of ESG ratings and rated entities. It is designed to be proportionate to firms' size and activities and is informed by international and existing standards. Firms that may be in scope should start preparing now. ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027. The FCA will provide webinars and access to its Pre-Application Support Service to help firms prepare. Firms should now: understand whether the framework could apply to their activities review the final rules and guidanceconsider whether they need FCA authorisationstart preparing for implementationengage early with FCA support servicesNotes to editorsRead the FCA’s Policy Statement and final rules, PS26/22, ‘ESG ratings: final regime’.The new framework takes effect on 29 June 2028. From that date, firms providing ESG ratings in the UK will need FCA authorisation and to have the relevant permission before carrying on that activity, unless an exemption applies.ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027. We are staggering application periods and encourage firms to apply as early as possible within their window. ESG ratings generally assess how companies or other entities, assets, or financial products perform against environmental, social and governance criteria. They are used by asset managers, lenders, benchmark administrators and others to inform capital allocation decisions and manage risk, among other uses. The approach is shaped by international standards, including recommendations from the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO). The final rules follow the FCA’s consultation, CP25/34, which opened on 1 December 2025 and closed on 31 March 2026. The regulatory framework follows government legislation bringing the provision of ESG ratings within the FCA’s remit in October 2025. 95% of respondents to the government’s consultation supported the move. The regime regulates how ESG ratings are produced, governed and communicated. It does not prescribe a particular sustainability view or methodology. There is strong investor demand for ESG information. The FCA's Financial Lives Survey 2024 found 72% of adults with investments or a defined contribution pension wanted their investments to do some good as well as provide a financial return.

title: FCA sets expectations for firms making car finance settlement offers
raw_summary: Research shows consumers want the choice, rather than wait for the legal challenges to conclude. Almost 9 out of 10 (89%) car finance customers who have complained or are considering doing so want the choice of an offer of compensation now, rather than waiting for the legal challenges to the FCA's compensation scheme to conclude. 86% would be comfortable making the decision, and 61% say they’d accept an offer in line with the scheme. Timing matters for many: 77% say receiving compensation sooner would make a great deal or fair amount of difference to their financial situation.The survey findings are being released today alongside the FCA's expectations for lenders who want to make settlement offers to those owed compensation under its scheme, while legal challenges continue. This comes as Barclays Partner Finance confirms it will make settlement offers to some of its customers owed compensation.The regulator supports lenders making settlement offers, as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme.Lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes that they will keep any money received, even if the outcome of the legal challenges means they would have received less. However, they also wouldn’t be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge means they would have been paid more. As consumers can reject an offer and leave their claim to be dealt with under the scheme, these offers can’t be referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service for review.Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA’s general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said:'Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. And it’s clear they want the choice.'Anyone who wants to wait can, and there’s no obligation to agree to the offer. We’ll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means.'To help consumers make informed decisions, the FCA has published a factsheet (PDF) that lenders must share with customers when making settlement offers. Not all lenders are likely to make offers, and those that do may only make them to some customers owed compensation. The FCA will regularly update its website with lenders making settlement offers to help consumers check whether an offer is genuine. Firms are expected to notify the FCA if they plan to make offers.Payouts under the motor finance compensation scheme were due to start this year. The scheme is currently partially suspended, pending the outcome of legal challenges due to be heard between 16 February and 3 March 2027. Under the partial suspension, firms must keep preparing for the scheme and continue progressing complaints as far as possible, but do not need to calculate or pay compensation under the scheme until the legal process concludes.Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained should complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free. There is no need to use a law firm or claims management company, which may charge up to 36% of any compensation, including VAT.Notes to editorsResearch conducted by Kantar, surveying 1,000 motor finance customers online between 25 and 28 June 2026. Findings cited are based on a subset of 590 respondents who said they had made or were considering making a motor finance complaint.Barclays press release.Statement confirming motor finance legal challenge to be heard in February 2027.Statement on the partial suspension of the motor finance scheme and what it means for firms and consumers.

title: Demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments
raw_summary: We have seen demands being made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries as a way to avoid tax. HMRC has sought to tackle this tax avoidance through what has been termed the loan charge and published guidance for those affected.Questions have been raised about the regulatory status of these loans and whether they were ever intended to be repaid.Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they’re unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.Some consumers are, however being sent legal letters threatening potential court action and asking for immediate repayment of the loan. Repayment is being sought after these disguised remuneration loans were sold by the original provider to a third party.Those seeking payment may ask the FCA to agree to a Validation Order. This is the formal permission needed before the loans could be enforced. We would consider any request carefully and our agreement is by no means guaranteed. If a Validation Order is required and not granted, the debt would remain unenforceable.Anyone who receives a demand for repayment of a disguised remuneration loan, and is unsure whether they are liable for the amount claimed, should consider carefully whether to make any payment. We’d encourage them to look at the HMRC guidance and consider taking legal advice.Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.If you are experiencing any difficulties, whether they are health, money or other difficulties, or if you don't understand what is happening, you should raise this with those contacting you.

title: FCA publishes terms of reference for independent review concerning Mr Andriesz
raw_summary: We have published the terms of reference for the review into our handling of interactions with Mr Simon Andriesz, a whistleblower who made protected disclosures to the FCA. We shared our condolences following Mr Andriesz's tragic death and our thoughts remain with his family and loved ones.The review was commissioned by our non-executive directors. It is being conducted by Lea Paterson CBE, an independent non-executive director of the FCA.When we announced the review, we said it would examine how we interacted with Mr Andriesz. The review will now also look at whether we met our responsibilities under whistleblowing law and followed our own policies and procedures when handling his whistleblowing reports, including his concerns that he had experienced detriment. It will cover the period from at least 2017 to 2026.The review will identify any lessons learned and make recommendations for improvements to our future engagement with external whistleblowers and vulnerable individuals.We previously said we aimed to publish findings in early 2027. Given this broader scope and the need to examine evidence spanning many years, more time is needed to complete the review thoroughly.A progress update will be published in January 2027, with the final report expected in spring 2027.Read the terms of reference (PDF).

title: Brits nearly twice as likely to spot pressure tactics in horror films as investment red flags
raw_summary: Investors are almost twice as likely to recognise pressure tactics in a horror film as they are when those tactics are used to promote an investment opportunity, new FCA data suggests. A survey of UK 18 to 40-year-olds who own or are considering investments found 65% spotted ‘this is your only chance’ as a classic horror warning sign. But when faced with a ‘last chance to buy’ investment opportunity, only 36% said it would make them more cautious, while 37% said they would feel pressure to buy quickly or risk missing out. The pattern also holds for other pressure tactics. While 59% recognised countdowns like the ticking clock in 'Saw' as a tactic designed to make characters act rashly, just 5% said they would be suspicious of the pressure created by a rising investment price graph.Blind spots show up with novelty, too. Nearly half (47%) recognised that horror sequels often bring back familiar threats disguised as something new. Yet only 12% were similarly sceptical of a 'groundbreaking new' investment product, while 1 in 10 said being new would actually make them more likely to invest. Peer pressure and hype also influenced attitudes towards investment. While 80% recognised ‘trust me, it's fine, everyone's doing it’ as a warning sign in a horror scenario, almost 3 in 10 (29%) said excitement from friends or group chats about an investment would reassure them or make them trust the opportunity rather than doing their own research. Lucy Castledine, director of consumer investments at the FCA, said: 'Many people can spot a horror movie trap a mile off, but this survey suggests they’re far less likely to recognise the same tactics when they're used to influence investment decisions. Hype, urgency and fear of missing out can all influence how people invest, so before acting on an opportunity, do your research and make sure it's right for you.'The FCA's InvestSmart campaign helps consumers make more informed investment decisions. Its Hype Type Revealer helps people understand what may influence their decisions and how to avoid being drawn in by investment hype.Note to editors Research conducted by Attest on behalf of the FCA. Fieldwork conducted on 9 October 2026. The sample comprised 666 respondents based in the UK, and was open to all adults across the 18 to 40 age range. All participants either currently own investments or would consider buying investments in the next 12 months.Additional findings from the research include:Around half of respondents hold a stocks and shares ISA.1 in 4 own cryptocurrency.Nearly 1 in 10 own NFTs.Initial testing of the Hype Type Revealer with more than 600 retail investors found its training intervention reduced high-risk investment decisions by 34.9%, even 7 days later.

title: What does 'fair value' look like in practice? Three years into the Consumer Duty, here’s what we’ve learned.
raw_summary: Fair value is a simple yet important principle at the heart of the Consumer Duty: the price customers pay should be reasonable, relative to the benefits they get. But applying that principle in practice requires judgement.Three years into the Consumer Duty, we’re seeing clear differences between firms that have embedded fair value into their approach and those that still need to strengthen their assessments, evidence and monitoring.We recently reviewed how firms across the consumer finance market assess, evidence and monitor fair value. We also carried out focused work on fees and charges across a range of credit products, and supervisory work on consumer hire and third-party ownership agreements for home energy infrastructure.Many firms are getting it right, building fair value into how they design, price and monitor their products. Others are missing things that, in hindsight, could have been avoidable. Where firms fell short, a recurring issue was the evidence supporting their conclusions.Here are 3 areas that separated the 2, and questions firms can use to challenge their approach to assessing and monitoring fair value.Does your evidence actually tell you something, or just describe your product?Across the firms and products we reviewed, stronger fair value assessments showed a clear, evidenced relationship between what customers paid and the benefits they could reasonably expect to receive. One credit card provider, for example, quantified the cashback, foreign exchange savings and other account benefits customers received, and set these directly against the fees and interest they paid. That gave them a clear evidence base for their fair value conclusion, not just a description of the product's features.Weaker assessments tended to rely on assumptions rather than actual customer data. Some had relevant evidence, but it was scattered across different documents and never brought together into a coherent picture. This made it hard for anyone, including us, to see how firms had reached their conclusions.Are you assessing fair value for different customer groups?Fair value isn't one-size-fits-all. Firms showing an understanding of that nuance segmented their customers by factors such as credit risk, product usage, distribution channel and characteristics of vulnerability, and assessed fair value across the resulting groups. Some firms also assessed fair value across different pricing groups, including APR bands and risk-based pricing groups, to understand whether customers paying different prices continued to receive fair value. Other firms treated their whole target market as a single, homogeneous group when testing fair value. This made it difficult to spot if some customers were quietly paying more, or getting less, than others, which is exactly the kind of thing a fair value assessment is supposed to identify.If customers can't picture the real cost, does the price even matter?Fair value also needs to be considered alongside customer understanding. Even a well-designed, fairly priced product can fall short if customers don't understand what they're signing up to. Some firms tested comprehension directly, including one that proactively contacted customers incurring certain charges to check they understood how and when those charges applied. This gave the firm evidence about whether customers understood the charges, rather than relying only on the existence or readability of disclosures.We also looked at consumer hire agreements for home energy equipment, where some promotions used 'pay as you save' claims that could lead customers to believe that savings or affordability were guaranteed. Those outcomes depended on factors such as equipment performance, changes in customers’ circumstances and future energy prices over agreements lasting up to 25 years. Firms should make these clear and avoid creating the impression that savings or affordability are assured.What this means for your firm Use these findings to challenge your approach to assessing and monitoring fair value. Ask:Does your evidence tell you something meaningful about customer outcomes, or does it simply describe your product?Does your target market behave as one group once you look closely?Can customers understand the total price they might pay and the financial commitment they are entering into?A common feature of stronger approaches was that firms supported their conclusions with evidence rather than relying on assumptions.The good news is that this doesn’t need to always require complex modelling or new data. Smaller firms may be able to draw on information they already hold, including complaints, arrears, customer feedback and product usage.If there's one thing to take from this, it's to show your working: what your evidence shows, how it supports your conclusion, what you'd do if it didn't.We expect firms to read the full findings. They also cover how firms assessed total price and benefits, used competitor benchmarking, and used controls to reduce the risk of foreseeable harm from fees and charges, including the home energy sector examples we touched on above.We'll keep monitoring this area through our supervisory work and will continue sharing what we learn as our understanding develops.

title: FCA stops HTX's crypto promotions
raw_summary: The FCA has secured High Court undertakings to ensure that HTX (formerly Huobi), a global crypto exchange, will not knowingly promote cryptoasset services unlawfully to UK consumers. The FCA took legal action against HTX in October 2025 for breaking UK financial promotion rules. HTX had failed repeatedly to engage with the FCA. Following the commencement of proceedings, HTX took steps to exit the UK. The FCA and Huobi Global S.A. have now reached a settlement in the case. HTX is no longer active in the UK. Consumers can no longer make deposits, and new UK users cannot sign up to the platform. HTX will not target, solicit or actively seek to engage UK consumers.UK users of HTX should read the information published on HTX's website about the availability of its services in the UK and the arrangements for withdrawing any residual assets.Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said: 'Crypto firms should be under no illusion: being based overseas does not put them beyond the reach of UK law. Our action means HTX is leaving the UK and can no longer target UK consumers. The message to other firms is clear: follow the rules or face the consequences.'Consumers should check a firm's permissions using the FCA Firm Checker and remember that cryptoassets are high-risk investments.Notes to editorsRead details of the proceedings and relevant court documents. Huobi Global S.A. is the first defendant in the proceedings.View the court order (PDF) containing the undertakings. Huobi Global's undertakings to the court include that it will not knowingly, directly or indirectly, communicate or cause to be communicated a financial promotion in contravention of section 21 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000. This covers the HTX website, software applications and social media platforms.The proceedings were commenced in the Business and Property Division of the High Court on 21 October 2025.The FCA publicly announced its enforcement action on 10 February 2026. The terms of the settlement are confidential. The settlement does not constitute an admission of liability or wrongdoing by Huobi Global or any other person or entity.Crypto is a high-risk investment and remains largely unregulated in the UK, except for anti-money laundering and financial promotions until October 2027. Use the FCA Firm Checker to check a firm’s permissions.

title: Bullseye Financial Ltd enters administration
raw_summary: On 23 October 2026, Bullseye Financial Ltd (Bullseye Financial) entered administration. Robert Young of Azets Holdings Limited and Matthew Haw of RSM UK Restructuring Advisory LLP were appointed as joint administrators. The joint administrators are responsible for managing the affairs of the firm during the administration process.Bullseye Financial is authorised by the FCA. It served only professional investors, either managing investment portfolios for them within agreed limits or carrying out their instructions to buy or sell investments without giving investment advice.On 11 March 2026, Bullseye Financial agreed to a voluntary requirement to stop carrying out any regulated activity.Below we set out:How to contact the joint administrators.Support for customers.What to do if you are concerned about your investments.What to do if you have a complaint with the firm.How to protect yourself from fraudsters claiming to act on behalf of the firm, the joint administrators or the FCA.Who to contact if you're a customerCustomers of Bullseye Financial can contact the joint administrators on:Phone: 02074 031877Email: BFL@azets.co.ukWebsite: www.azets.com/en-uk/bullseye-financial-ltdAddress: Azets Holdings Limited, 5th Floor, 16 Great Queen Street, London WC2B 5DG.Protect yourself from scamsFraudsters sometimes claim to be from legitimate firms authorised by us, or (in the case of administration) their appointed administrator.Be wary of fraudsters pretending to be from Bullseye Financial or the joint administrators and asking you to pay money to get your money back.If you get an unexpected call from someone claiming to be from Bullseye Financial or the joint administrators, you should: End the call straight away.Call them back using the phone number above.Find out how to protect yourself from scams, including recovery room scams.

title: Defence SMEs need banking services that work
raw_summary: The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusionThe current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.Defence is not one-size-fits-allThere is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.Better information leads to better decisionsAnother theme that stood out was the importance of data.Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:Are applications taking longer than expected?Are decisions being applied consistently?Do governance processes reflect actual risk?Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.Getting the balance rightOur work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.Read our findings.

title: Chandler King (City) Limited enters creditors’ voluntary liquidation

title: FCA calls on private market firms to manage conflicts of interest in line with rapid growth
raw_summary: Private market firms vary in how well they identify and manage conflicts of interest, according to an FCA review. Private markets refer to investments in assets, companies, or debt not listed or traded on public exchanges. They’ve grown significantly in recent years, and the UK is a leading international centre. Private markets play an increasingly important role in providing capital to businesses and opportunities for returns to investors. Private markets can give rise to conflicts that differ from those in public markets, and effective disclosure is important to enable investors to assess whether their interests are being protected.The FCA found examples of good practice by firms across private equity, private credit and real estate asset classes. These included strong governance arrangements, effective oversight and independent challenge. It also identified some areas where firms could strengthen governance, oversight and conflicts management arrangements to support fair investor outcomes.As private markets grow and business models become more complex, the FCA found that some firms were failing to identify conflicts adequately or keep their controls up to date. Recurring weaknesses were identified in areas including cross-fund transfers and multi-party transactions, gifts and entertainment, and information barriers.The FCA expects firms to be able to identify, record, manage and disclose conflicts effectively, and demonstrate that investors are being treated fairly, particularly in areas where investors place significant reliance on firms' judgement, governance and controls.Michelle Beck, director of wholesale buy-side at the FCA, said: 'Firms need to ensure their management of conflicts of interest keeps pace with growth in their size and complexity. We found good practice across the sector, but standards varied considerably. We want to encourage confidence in the UK’s private markets. Firms should act on our findings and identify where they can strengthen controls.'Although not part of this review, the FCA is examining governance and conflicts concerns relating to the use of private credit to fund consumer litigation claims, including significant risks of harm to investors, consumers and markets.Notes to editorsConflicts of interest and fair customer treatment in private markets.The review examined how firms identify, manage, mitigate and disclose conflicts of interest across private equity, private credit and real estate markets.The report includes examples of both good practice and areas where firms could strengthen arrangements.The review forms part of the FCA's wider supervisory focus on private markets and investor outcomes.

title: Beyond borders: Regulating the risks we share
raw_summary: Speech by Ashley Alder, FCA Chair, at the Michael D. Gill Lecture on International Financial Regulatory Understanding and Cooperation. I wasn’t fortunate enough to work as closely with Mike as many of you in this room.But I knew him well enough during my time with the IOSCO board to appreciate someone who was kind and unassuming, whilst being absolutely determined to make lives better through his work.He personified the very best attributes of dedicated public service.In his 2024 lecture Andrew Bailey described Mike as a passionate internationalist, and reflected on what this meant for the UK after the Brexit referendum.Two years on, the values that Mike championed are even more on point.Mike understood implicitly that relationships between regulators are about so much more than institutional goodwill – they depend on trust, candour and constructive practical action.That’s an aspect of his legacy that is just as relevant – perhaps even more so – today.In an increasingly interconnected global financial system, no institution can see the whole picture on its own.Success depends not only on what each regulator does individually, but on what we can see, understand, test, and address together.

title: FCA restricts 6 firms following concerns over anti-money laundering controls
raw_summary: Restrictions have been placed on 6 unregulated lenders, known as Annex 1 firms, after the FCA raised concerns about their anti-money laundering policies, controls and procedures while assessing their applications. The restrictions were imposed by the FCA on each firm’s request and limit their ability to take on new customers or do new business with existing customers, including extending existing credit.This action forms part of the FCA’s enhanced oversight of Annex 1 firms. These firms operate in sectors that can present a heightened risk of money laundering and other financial crime and are required to register with the FCA for supervision under the Money Laundering Regulations. They are not authorised or subject to wider FCA regulation.The FCA has previously warned Annex 1 firms that they will be subject to increased scrutiny. They must be able to demonstrate they understand the financial crime risks they face and have effective systems and controls in place to manage those risks, or face action.More widely, the FCA is assessing responses to an information request sent to around 900 registered Annex 1 firms to identify and disrupt financial crime risks and determine where further action is needed.The FCA has also reminded regulated firms that, when dealing with Annex 1 firms, they must carry out due diligence to understand the firm’s business, in accordance with legislative requirements. This includes seeking direct confirmation from the firm of its registration status, conducting independent checks of the information it provides, and understanding and managing any risks.Registration under the Money Laundering Regulations is not a substitute for regulated firms carrying out their own appropriate due diligence.Steve Smart, executive director lead for fighting financial crime at the FCA, said: 'We have warned Annex 1 firms that they face increased scrutiny. They must demonstrate they can manage the money laundering risks they face. Where they cannot satisfy us, we will intervene.'Notes to editorsVoluntary restrictions were imposed on Kingscrown Finance Ltd on 21 April 2026, with further voluntary restrictions imposed on 25 September 2026. The further restrictions limit how Kingscrown may receive payments from existing customers and require an orderly wind-down of its existing loan book.On 7 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on MOMSB Ltd and Momentus Capital Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements subject to limited exceptions, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.On 9 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Grosvenor Funding Ltd and Grosvenor Funding (North West) Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.On 15 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Abbital Ltd. The restrictions specify the circumstances in which Abbital may take on new customers, enter into new lending arrangements or accept payments from existing customers. They also require an independent review of Abbital’s anti-money laundering systems and controls.Fighting financial crime is one of the FCA's strategic priorities.

title: Market integrity in a digital age
raw_summary: Speech by Nikhil Rathi, FCA chief executive at the Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner, Mansion House. The success of the UK’s financial servicesIn August, flight cancellations left my sons and I with an extra day in Boston. A Red Sox game, perhaps?No, the Rathi boys – naturally – headed straight to…the Museum of American Finance.Funded by industry, the museum celebrates the role of finance in American life.Illuminating the powerful benefits of informed risk taking.Three sceptical boys engrossed for nearly 2 hours. I quite enjoyed it too.It struck me though how right George Bernard Shaw was: Britain and America are 2 countries separated by a common language.On this side of the pond, we’re perhaps more reserved, embarrassed even, talking about why finance matters.Yet there’s plenty to cheer.We are the world’s biggest cross-border banking, foreign exchange (FX) and derivatives trading centre. We’re second in investment management … And our commercial insurance sector has doubled in size over a decade…A financial services sector built on trust and one the whole United Kingdom should be proud of… Even more so as new technologies, so many owing to our research base, transform our economy and society.UK firms leading in:artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and tokenisation.consumer access to investment opportunities widened.moving from Open Banking to Open Finance.Lady Mayor, your myth busting campaigns have championed London and the City.Thank you for your leadership.If we can capture this opportunity, we gain in productivity… With rewards of economic growth felt across the country.

title: Leeds office move
raw_summary: We have signed an agreement for a new office at 2 Wellington Place, which will become our long-term home in Leeds from 2028. The new office will provide 36,097 sq ft of space for our growing Leeds presence.Our Leeds office, currently at 6 Queen Street, has continued to grow since opening in 2022.Securing a new permanent base reflects our commitment to the city and supports our 5-year strategy ambition to have 1,000 roles based outside London by 2030.There is still some time before the move, and we'll share more about our new office and plans closer to 2028.

title: b12128
raw_summary: tests: fix CI flakes of TOPK_MOE caused by near ties ( #31426 ) tests: fix CI flakes of TOPK_MOE caused by near ties With uniform random logits, two experts sometimes land within one f32 ulp of each other at a routing boundary, mostly with sqrt_softplus gating whose output range is narrow. A backend whose gating differs by a few ulps from the CPU then picks the other expert and the test fails. Draw each row of logits again until the group selection and the final top-k both have a relative margin of 1e-4, computed on the host in double precision. tests: build the TOPK_MOE logits by inverting the gating function Draw the selection scores (probs plus bias) of each row as a random permutation of a grid, move the experts of the best groups up by half a step, and set the logits to the inverse of the gating function at these scores. Every expert and group decision is then one grid step apart on all backends, and the host no longer recomputes the routing. The softmax probs are built to sum to one so that the softmax keeps the scores, and the views of the logits are not initialized again after the logits are set. title: b12127: metal: keep fusable node groups inside one command buffer (#31688)
raw_summary: The first command buffer takes the first 10% of the graph nodes and the rest is split evenly between the extra command buffers. A fusion cannot span two command buffers, so a boundary that falls inside a fusable group runs that group unfused, and the output then depends on the node count of the graph. Move each boundary to the end of the fusable group it falls into, so the encoders fuse the same nodes as with a single command buffer.

title: b12126: qwen2 : add nvfp4 scales to build_ffn (#31657)
raw_summary: This commit adds nvfp4 scales to qwen2's build_ffn call which are currently passed as NULL. The motivation for this is that a model converted to NVFP4 will currently crash because the scales are loaded but never applied in the FFN: llama-completion: llama.cpp/src/llama-sampler.cpp:1218: void llama_sampler_dist_apply(llama_sampler*, llama_token_data_array*): Assertion `found' failed. The attention already applies its scales but ffn is missing them.
